procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 14, 1963 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 380 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Magistrate acquitted the accused. The Corporation (State) appealed to the Calcutta High Court under s. 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court allowed the appeal against the appellants (Baburally and firm) but dismissed it against the remaining accused persons.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (Baburally and firm) appealed to the Supreme Court with certificate (presumably a certificate of fitness for appeal granted by the High Court).

issue.issue_text: Whether the defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 was available to the appellants, who were found storing and selling condensed milk that was below the prescribed standard.

facts: The appellants were prosecuted for storing and selling condensed milk after a sample taken from their shop was found to be adulterated.
The Public Analyst determined the milk's fat content was 3.4%, which is below the minimum prescribed standard of 9%.
The appellants argued they were protected by the defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
They claimed that the label on the tins, which described the product as "Full cream sweetened condensed milk," served as a warranty.
law: Section 19(2) of the Act provides a defense to a vendor who is ignorant of the quality of the food sold.
To successfully use this defense, a vendor must prove, among other things, that:
1. The food sold was the 'same in nature, substance and quality as that demanded by the purchaser'.
2. The vendor had purchased the food with a 'written warranty in the prescribed form'.
application: The Court reasoned that for the milk to be considered 'condensed milk' under the Act, it must meet the prescribed standard (9% fat).

Since the appellants' milk was below this standard, it could not be legally regarded as 'condensed milk' and was therefore not the 'same in nature, substance and quality' as what a purchaser demanding condensed milk would expect.
The Court also determined that the label on the tin was merely a description of the product and did not constitute a 'written warranty in the prescribed form' as required by the law.
The label did not certify that the food met the specific legal standards demanded by the vendor.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' defense under Section 19(2). It held that the defense was not available because the appellants failed to meet two essential requirements: the milk was substandard and therefore not the same as what was demanded, and they did not have a warranty in the legally prescribed form.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 was available to the appellants, who were found storing and selling condensed milk that was below the prescribed standard.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that they were protected by the defense in Section 19(2) of the Act.
They claimed to have purchased the tins of condensed milk from a trader, Messrs S. Choudhury Brothers, and were told that the label on each tin served as the required warranty.

They contended that the label, which described the milk as 'Full cream sweetened condensed milk' and stated it was 'pure and produced from healthy cow's milk,' was a warranty within the meaning of the Act.
The appellants asserted that they sold the tins in the same condition in which they were purchased and had no reason to believe that the nature, substance, or quality of the milk had been altered.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the court, was that the defense under Section 19(2) could not succeed because the appellants failed to prove they had purchased the articles with a 'written warranty in the prescribed form' as required by the law.

It was argued that the label on the tin was merely a description of the food and did not constitute a legal warranty certifying that the food was of the nature, substance, and quality demanded by the vendor.

The words 'Full Cream' on the label were insufficient to satisfy the legal requirements, as the term was not defined in the Act and the label did not provide enough information to calculate the fat content.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a vendor to successfully use the defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, they must prove the article of food was purchased with a written warranty in the prescribed form. A label on the product can only serve as a warranty if it contains a specific certification as required by the rules; a generic, undefined description on the label is insufficient. A vendor who accepts and sells an article with a legally deficient label cannot claim to have had no reason to believe the product was not of the prescribed quality, and the fact that the article was sold in the same state as it was purchased is not, by itself, a sufficient defense.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act was unavailable to the appellants because the label on the tins of condensed milk did not constitute the legally required "written warranty in the prescribed form." The court found that the appellants had failed to prove the existence of such a warranty, and the fact that they sold the tins in the same condition as purchased was, by itself, insufficient to absolve them of liability for selling an adulterated product.
legal_tests_applied: To successfully claim the defense under Section 19(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, a vendor must prove they purchased the article of food with a "written warranty in the prescribed form."
A vendor must also show they "had no reason to believe" that the article of food was not of the prescribed nature, substance, and quality.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to prove that they had purchased the condensed milk with a written warranty as required by the Act; the court explicitly stated, regarding the label, "There is not a whisper of any warranty on it."
The court rejected the argument that the label itself served as a warranty, viewing it merely as a description of the product.
The fact that the appellants "sold the tins in the same state as they purchased them... was by itself not sufficient to absolve them."
The court determined that a vendor accepting tins with such a label "cannot be said to have 'had no reason to believe' that it was not condensed milk of the prescribed nature, substance and quality."
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's position that the defense under Section 19(2) could not succeed because the appellants failed to prove they had purchased the articles with a written warranty.

It was established as a matter of fact that the condensed milk was adulterated, as its fat content was only 3.4% whereas the prescribed minimum was 9%, constituting a clear breach of Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Act.
The High Court was found to be correct in setting aside the initial acquittal and convicting the appellants for the offense.
